problems.prompt: Why is the field inside a hollow conductor placed in an external electric field exactly zero in electrostatic equilibrium?
choices: Free charges redistribute on the conductor's surface until their field cancels the external field inside
The conductor absorbs the field lines and converts them to heat
Electric fields cannot exist near any solid object
The interior is always grounded to zero potential
problems.explain: Mobile free charges move to the surface and rearrange until the net field inside the conductor (and any cavity it encloses) is zero — that is what 'electrostatic equilibrium' means.

problems.prompt: For a conducting mesh cage, shielding gets ____ (better/worse) as the hole size relative to the cage grows larger.
problems.explain: Larger gaps let more of the external field leak through, so the shielding factor S drops and the interior field rises.

problems.prompt: Why doesn't an insulating enclosure shield its interior from an external electric field?
choices: It has no free charges that can redistribute to cancel the field
It amplifies the external field instead of blocking it
Insulators are always thinner than conductors
Electric fields cannot pass through any material, including insulators
problems.explain: Shielding relies on mobile free charges rearranging on a conductor's surface; an insulator's charges are bound and cannot move to cancel the interior field, so the external field passes through essentially undisturbed.

problems.prompt: If the external field is E₀ = 10 kV/m and the interior field measured is E_in = 0.1 kV/m, what is the shielding effectiveness SE = 20·log₁₀(E₀/E_in) in dB?
